newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi forces said undeterred in rebel north.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi forces said undeterred in rebel north.

text.p: Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani, newly allied with President Saddam Hussein, on Tuesday echoed Baghdad's defiance of U.S. military might and said his alliance was forced by the United States.

And Barzani's Kurdish rival -- who was thrown out of the city of Arbil at the weekend by Iraqi troops supporting Barzani's militia -- said that Iraqi troops and tanks were still deployed in the region.

"Forty Iraqi tanks, as well as artillery, moved from Qushtapa toward Bustaneh... Their advance has been stopped by the peshmerga (guerrilla) resistance," rival Kurdish leader Jelal Talabani told Reuters by telephone from his stronghold of Sulaimaniya, more than 100 km (60 miles) to the southeast.

Barzani told a press conference his faction had grown impatient with U.S. promises to nurture Kurdish autonomy in northern Iraq, which since the 1991 Gulf War has been protected by a U.S.-led allied force from attacks by Baghdad.
"It is for...years the Americans have played with us and have been onlookers," said Barzani in his stronghold of Salahuddin.
"I am not afraid of the cruise missiles," Barzani said in Kurdish through an interpreter.
Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) at the weekend joined up with Iraqi troops to oust Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) from the region's main city of Arbil.
The United States on Tuesday launched cruise missile strikes on southern Iraq in retaliation for the Iraqi attacks on Kurds in the mainly Kurdish northern Iraq.

But Baghdad appeared unbowed by U.S. missile strikes, deploying armour and artillery against Kurdish rebels and unleashing its secret police against the fallen city of Arbil, opposition sources in northern said.
Talabani said Iraqi troop movements occured after U.S. cruise missiles were launched against military targets in southern Iraq -- about 1000 km (600 miles) away from the Kurdish-held north.
The umbrella opposition Iraqi National Congress (INC), meanwhile, said scores of people had been rounded up in Arbil, capital of the predominantly Kurdish north.
"Hundreds of people have already been rounded up by Saddam's secret police and are facing torture and death," INC leader Ahmad Chelabi said in London.

"We would welcome any further action to force Saddam to pull out all his forces from northern Iraq including tanks, artillery, troops and especially secret police agents," Chalabi said in a statement welcoming U.S. intervention.
A spokesman in Turkey for Iraq's minority Turkomans said about 2,000 of his countrymen had been arrested and deported in trucks from Arbil to Mosul, an oil centre under Baghdad's central control.
"We fear for their lives," said Hasan Ozmen in Ankara.
It was impossible to verify the charges of mass arrests, and even public executions, by the secret police. Reporters have been barred from Arbil by Barzani's forces, which now control the city.
Talabani's faction had held the city since 1994, when an uneasy Kurdish alliance collapsed in fighting.
